newsitem.title: UK: Strike-hit BA to operate 20 pct more flights.
newsitem.headline: Strike-hit BA to operate 20 pct more flights.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Thursday it expected to operate 20 percent more flights than on Wednesday, as a 72-hour strike by cabin crew, which stranded 25,000 passengers yesterday, entered its second day.
"We expect to run 20 percent more flights today and another 20 percent more tomorrow (the last day of the strike)," BA spokesman David Budgen told Reuters.
BA said it was still considering legal action against the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) over the legality of the cabin crew strike ballot.

Of its long-haul flights from London Heathrow, BA expects to operate 53 percent of its normal service while on short-haul services it will run 15 percent of flights out of Terminal Four. For short-haul flights from Terminal One it will offer 27 percent of normal service.
At London Gatwick, BA said it had no cancellations to short-haul flights, while it was running half of long-haul services.

The T&G, acting for the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association (BASSA) said there was "solid support" for the second day of the walk-out. The strike is being held over a new pay structure BA has implemented as part of a massive cost-saving drive.
The T&G says it will call another 72-hour strike if no agreement is reached with management. BA says the "ball is firmly in the unions court" regarding the negotiation process.
BA said 189 cabin crew had so far gone on strike, while 1,000 cabin crew had reported in for work. Under UK aviation rules, airlines need one member of staff for every 50 passengers.

Another 1,549 cabin crew had reported in sick to date, of which 163 had called in last night to say they would not be coming in to work, rather than admit they were striking for fear of reprisals from the airline.

Management has warned that employees face loss of travel perks and opportunities of promotion if they went on strike. It has also threatened to sack or even sue individual strikers -- tactics which the unions have termed "intimidatory" and "macho".
In a further move which will pressurise strikers, BA told Reuters it had 500 new cabin crew recruits ready to come in, while another 3,000 had applied for jobs.
BA's Budgen said the airline, one of the world's biggest and most successful, continued to believe the strike ballot held by the T&G last month was illegal.
It says there is a discrepancy in the number of cabin crew staff who took part in the strike ballot -- some 9,000 -- and the number registered on the company payroll -- 7,800.

"We are in active discussion with our lawyers to decide our next action...The T&G replied to our letter (pointing out the apparent discrepancy in the balloting process), they've disagreed with us but we know this strike is unlawful," he said.

George Ryde, the union's senior aviation official, told the UK Press Association news agency the union believed its ballot of cabin crew for industrial action was legal and would be upheld in court if BA decided to mount a challenge.
"We have gone back through our balloting arrangements and we are confident they were entirely legal," Ryde said.
Meanwhile, a decision is expected later today from BA ground staff belonging to the T&G on whether to stage a separate strike in protest at the sale of the airline's catering operation at Heathrow.
